name: Temperate rainforest
notes: Cool, very wet coastal forest of giant evergreen conifers (or southern beeches) with a dense fern-and-shrub understory and every trunk draped in moss and lichen; drawn on the Pacific Northwest, Valdivian Chile, New Zealand and Hokkaido.

emergent.name: Coast redwood

growth.juvenile_note: Seedling with 2 (rarely 3-4) cotyledons on a thin red stem; flat, dark-green, 15-25 mm needles in two flat ranks like a yew spray. Sapling a narrow cone with drooping branch tips and a nodding leader, can add 0.6-2 m a year. Burl buds form in the cotyledon axils, so even young trees resprout rings of shoots from the base.
growth.source: USDA Silvics of N America vol. 1 (Olson et al.): seed at 5-15 yr, 30-46 m at 50 yr and 50-67 m at 100 yr on good sites, oldest ~2,200 yr, very tolerant, vigorous sprouting; USDA Woody Plant Seed Manual Sequoia (21-day germination test); Wikipedia (juvenile flat leaves 15-25 mm)

emergent.source: N California fog belt; tallest tree on Earth; resprouts from the stump. Kew POWO.

growth.source: USDA Silvics (Harris): ~27 m within 50 years of reaching breast height on average SE Alaska sites; cones occasionally before 20 yrs, in stands from 20-40; good crops every 3-8 years; tolerant of shade (less than hemlock); may live 700-800 years

canopy.name: Western redcedar

growth.juvenile_note: Tiny epigeal seedlings, often on rotting logs, first bear sharp, needle-like juvenile leaves, then flat sprays of overlapping scale leaves. Saplings survive deep shade as narrow, drooping-tipped cones; old trees build a huge fluted, buttressed trunk with stringy red-brown bark and branches that sweep down and turn up at the tips like candelabras, often with several dead spike tops.
growth.source: USDA Silvics of North America vol. 1 (Minore): germination within weeks in spring; cone production from 15-25 years, good crops every 3 years; very shade tolerant; slow-growing, commonly 50-70 m; lives over 1,000 years

The slow, dark trunk rises only after several years, clad in the stubs of old frond stalks, often with a skirt of dead fronds.

shrub.name: Pontic rhododendron

growth.juvenile_note: Dust-fine seed sprouts in light on moss, rotting wood, bare peat or scuffed acid soil that stays damp. The seedling is a tiny pair of seed leaves, then a thin sprig crowned with a few small dark leaves; slow for its first years, it thickens into a crooked, many-stemmed bush whose low branches root where they touch the ground, so one plant becomes a dark, dome-shaped thicket.
growth.source: Cross 1975, Biological Flora of the British Isles: Rhododendron ponticum (J. Ecol.), and the British and Irish invasion literature: dust-fine, wind-blown seed germinates in light on moss, bare peat or disturbed acid soil that stays damp; seedlings grow slowly at first; the plant layers where branches touch the ground, resprouts from the base when cut and casts shade dense enough to suppress the ground flora. Germination time, growth curve, first flowering and age estimated.

repro.note: low branches root where they touch the ground (layering), which here plays the sucker's part: neighbouring stems of a thicket are often one clone; cut stems resprout from the base

shrub.source: Rhododendron ponticum L., Pontic rhododendron: evergreen shrub or small tree 2-8 m that forms dense thickets in the understory of the humid Euxine-Colchic forests (oriental beech, oriental spruce) on the Black Sea slopes of northern Turkey and the Caucasus, west to Strandzha, with relict populations in southwest Iberia (subsp. baeticum) and Lebanon; acid soils only, shade-tolerant; naturalised and invasive in Britain and Ireland. Every part carries grayanotoxins: with R. luteum it is the nectar source of the Black Sea's mad honey (deli bal). Kew POWO for the name; Flora Europaea; Flora of Turkey (Davis); Cross 1975, Biological Flora of the British Isles (J. Ecol.).

traits.native_range: Black Sea forests of northern Turkey and the western Caucasus; relicts in southwest Iberia and Lebanon

traits.note: written for this species (the mad-honey rhododendrons)

bark.notes: grey-brown to red-brown, thin, smooth on young stems and finely flaking on old ones; crooked stems that root where they touch the ground

flower.form: rounded trusses of broad funnel-bells at the shoot tips, pale mauve to purple, the upper lobe freckled greenish-yellow, May-June
flower.notes: Mad honey: the nectar carries grayanotoxins (chiefly grayanotoxin I and III). Honeybees working these trusses in the Black Sea forests of Turkey and Georgia make deli bal, a dark, bitter honey taken by the spoonful as a folk tonic; more brings dizziness, a slow heart and low blood pressure (mad honey poisoning), rarely fatal. Xenophon's Anabasis (IV.8) tells of the Greek army felled by it near Trapezus (Trabzon) about 400 BC. R. luteum's nectar goes into the same honey.

fruit.form: woody brown capsules about 2 cm, clustered on the old truss, splitting from the top to shed dust-fine seed through the winter

appearance.seasonal: evergreen; the new shoots flush after flowering
appearance.silhouette: dark glossy domed thickets under beech, mauve in late spring
appearance.refs: Flora Europaea; Flora of Turkey (Davis); Kew POWO; Cross 1975, Biological Flora of the British Isles: Rhododendron ponticum (J. Ecol.); Jansen et al. 2012, Grayanotoxin poisoning: 'mad honey disease' and beyond (Cardiovasc. Toxicol.); Xenophon, Anabasis IV.8

fruiting.source: Flora Europaea; Flora of Turkey (Davis); Cross 1975: terminal trusses of broad funnel-bell flowers, pale mauve to purple with greenish-yellow spotting on the upper lobe, in late spring; a woody capsule that ripens in autumn and sheds dust-fine seed through the winter. Bumblebees are its main pollinators where it is naturalised in Britain and Ireland; honeybee visits carry the grayanotoxin nectar into mad honey. Truss size, capsule size, ripening time, set, crop and decay estimated.

shrub.name: Yellow azalea

growth.juvenile_note: Dust-fine seed sprouts in light on bare or mossy acid ground. The seedling is a tiny sprig of soft, hairy leaves that falls bare each autumn; within a few years it branches low into a twiggy little bush of upright grey-brown stems, the young shoots sticky with glandular hairs.
growth.source: Flora Europaea; Flora of Turkey (Davis): a deciduous shrub of forest edges, clearings and open woodland. Seed as for the genus: dust-fine, germinating on the surface in light. Germination time, growth curve, first flowering, age and suckering estimated.

Azalea pontica L., R. flavum G.Don), yellow or Pontic azalea: deciduous shrub 1.5-4 m of forest edges, clearings and open woodland in the Caucasus and northern Turkey, with relict outliers in eastern Europe (Poland, Belarus, Ukraine, Slovenia), the northern ones in open pine and oak woods on acid sandy soil; very fragrant, sticky, bright yellow funnel flowers in spring before or with the leaves; hairy leaves that turn crimson and orange in autumn. Every part carries grayanotoxins: with R. ponticum it is the nectar source of the Black Sea's mad honey (deli bal). Kew POWO for the name; Flora Europaea; Flora of Turkey (Davis).

growth.juvenile_note: Seeds are embedded in the green, fleshy spadix and drop into mud or float off in floods. The seedling is a small tuft of 1-3 bright green, oval to spoon-shaped leaves on short stalks from a thickening vertical rhizome, a miniature of the adult; each year the rosette grows until it carries huge upright paddle leaves up to 1.5 m. The first yellow hooded spathes appear after about 3-5 years.
growth.source: Oxford Univ. Plants 400 (sets seed after ~5 yr; rove-beetle pollinated; water-dispersed seed); Invasive Species Scotland (only plants 3+ yr old flower; seed bank viable 8-9 yr; slow growing); Wikipedia (leaves 30-150 cm); lifespan estimated

ground.name: Stair-step moss

growth.juvenile_note: Young plants are small loose wefts of red-stemmed, feathery, olive to golden-green fronds creeping over humus, logs or rock. Each year a new frond arches up from the middle of last year's, so a shoot becomes a staircase of flat, fern-like steps, one per year, the oldest dying brown underneath. A deep carpet rebuilds only slowly after fire, once a canopy has closed.
growth.source: Trees for Life (new segment each year from the centre of the previous one, segments live up to ~8 yr, sporophytes uncommon, slow recolonisation after fire, shade-loving); Wikipedia (one step per year used to age shoots). Lifespan is for the patch; spore-to-plant time and first capsule age estimated.

repro.note: spores by wind and water; no flowers; needs a wet film to reproduce, so spread reads moisture not pollinators

ground.source: Boreal and temperate rainforest; one storey per year, so its age is readable. Kew POWO.

ground.name: Sword fern

growth.juvenile_note: Spores sprout on moist humus or rotting logs into heart-shaped prothalli; the first fronds are tiny and simple to few-lobed, then short, once-pinnate fronds with small, eared, bristle-toothed pinnae. A young plant is a small evergreen rosette of a few stiff, dark green fronds from a short upright rhizome, adding fronds each spring until it becomes the big fountain-shaped clump.
growth.source: USDA FEIS Polystichum munitum (spores first produced at 1-5 yr; fronds 20-250 cm, sometimes 75-100 per plant, evergreen for several years; optimum under 3% light, grows in up to 40% sun); Wikipedia (fronds 50-180 cm, live 1.5-2.5 yr). Clump growth rate and lifespan estimated.

repro.note: spores by wind and water; no flowers; needs a wet film to reproduce, so spread reads moisture not pollinators

epiphyte.silhouette: shaggy moss drapes hanging from limbs

growth.juvenile_note: Starts as a green protonemal film and tiny shoots on bark, or from broken shoots lodged in branch crotches. Shoots creep along the bark, then send out long, dangling, whip-like stolons clothed in tiny leaves, so over years a patch becomes a shaggy, pendent curtain of golden-green, cat-tail-like strands hanging from maple and alder limbs.
growth.source: Wikipedia (Isothecium myosuroides group: epiphytic on rocks and trees, prefers broadleaf trees in humid forest); timings estimated from typical pleurocarpous epiphytic moss growth (a few cm per year) in Pacific Northwest rainforest.

epiphyte.name: Hanging moss

growth.juvenile_note: Spores give a green, thread-like protonema on bark; small upright shoots follow as a thin golden-green fuzz on twigs. Shoots then lengthen and droop into slender, pendent, sparsely branched strands with tiny closely pressed leaves, golden-orange to yellow-brown, hanging in curtains from branches in wet forest.
growth.source: Estimated from pendent epiphytic mosses (Meteoriaceae) of humid Australasian forests: spore-to-shoot time and strand growth of a few cm a year inferred from hanging-moss growth studies; no species-specific data found

repro.note: spores by wind and water; no flowers; needs a wet film to reproduce, so spread reads moisture not pollinators

growth.juvenile_note: Spores germinate in wet moss on bark or rock into small heart-shaped prothalli; the first fronds are tiny and simple, then lobed and once-pinnatifid with pointed segments. The scaly brown, licorice-sweet rhizome creeps through moss on bigleaf maple trunks and limbs, sending up single fronds in a row. Fronds appear with the autumn rains, stay green all winter and wither in summer drought.
growth.source: Wikipedia Polypodium glycyrrhiza (fronds usually 30-60 cm; creeping licorice-flavoured rhizome; on ground, rocks or as an epiphyte on moss-covered Acer macrophyllum; summer-deciduous, grows in the wet season; sori in two rows). Spore-to-plant time, growth and longevity estimated from Polypodium.

epiphyte.name: Lungwort lichen

growth.juvenile_note: A new thallus starts from a soredium or a broken lobe lodged on bark of an old tree in humid forest. It grows a few millimetres to a couple of centimetres a year into broad, leathery, lettuce-like lobes with a raised network of ridges and pits like lung tissue, bright green when wet and olive-brown when dry, plastered over trunks and branches.
growth.source: Wikipedia Lobaria pulmonaria and Brodo, Sharnoff & Sharnoff Lichens of North America (foliose, lobes to 7 cm wide, thalli 5-30 cm and more; mainly asexual by soredia and isidia, sexual maturity at about 25 years; indicator of old, unpolluted, humid forest). Ages estimated

repro.note: a lichen: fungus plus alga; spreads mostly by broken fragments and soredia/isidia carried by wind, water and animals; spores need to meet the right alga again

epiphyte.source: Lobaria pulmonaria, lungwort lichen: large leafy (foliose) lichen of old, humid broadleaf and conifer forest across the northern hemisphere, abundant in the Pacific Northwest rainforest; ridged and pitted green lobes like lung tissue. Index Fungorum for the name; Brodo, Sharnoff & Sharnoff Lichens of North America.

epiphyte.name: Old man's beard

growth.juvenile_note: New plants start mostly as broken-off fragments snagged on conifer twigs in humid, foggy lower canopies. A fragment is one pale grey-green, mostly unbranched thread densely set with short, even side fibrils at right angles, like a fine bottle-brush; it lengthens from the tips and drapes down, sometimes doubling in a year, and breaks into pieces that start new strands. Spore cups are rare.
growth.source: Wikipedia (Dolichousnea longissima): strands usually 15-30 cm, up to 3 m, can double its length each year, reproduces mainly by fragmentation, spore structures rarely seen, in canopies of old-growth conifer forest with high rainfall, humidity and fog. Ages and establishment times estimated.

repro.note: spores by wind and water; no flowers; needs a wet film to reproduce, so spread reads moisture not pollinators

epiphyte.source: Old-growth conifer forest; metre-long pale strands; only in clean, old, foggy forest — an age indicator. Index Fungorum.

epiphyte.name: Slender mouse-tail moss

growth.juvenile_note: Starts as a green protonemal film or a broken shoot lodged on bark or rock. Creeping stems send up crowded, curved, tree-like branches clothed in tiny pointed leaves, so a patch becomes a glossy yellow-green weft of arching little 'mouse tails' over tree bases, trunks and boulders.
